body: Do not send a message that is too long. Suppliers skim. Do not ask for a catalog right away – you will get a PDF and no quote. Do not say 'I am a small buyer' – it invites a higher price. And never give your full business plan in the first message.

faqs.q: Should I message in Chinese or English on Alibaba?
faqs.a: English is fine for most suppliers on Alibaba. They have English-speaking sales staff. If you want to build a closer relationship or negotiate on WeChat, a bit of Chinese helps, but it is not required for a first quote.

faqs.q: What is MOQ and why does it matter?
faqs.a: MOQ stands for Minimum Order Quantity. It is the smallest number of units a supplier will produce or sell. It matters because it sets the floor for your order and affects the unit price. Ask for it in your first message so you know if the supplier is a fit.

faqs.q: How long should I wait for a reply?
faqs.a: Most serious suppliers reply within 24 hours, often within a few hours. If you hear nothing in 48 hours, send a polite follow-up. If you still hear nothing, move on to the next supplier. There are thousands on Alibaba.

faqs.q: What if the supplier asks for my company details before quoting?
faqs.a: That is normal. They want to verify you are a real business. You can share your company name and website if you have one. If you are a solo importer, say you are a private buyer. Do not give your passport or bank details – that is a red flag.

faqs.q: Can I negotiate the MOQ down?
faqs.a: Yes, you can ask. Say something like 'Your MOQ is 1000, but I can only start with 300. Can you do a trial order at a higher unit price?' Many suppliers will agree to a smaller first order to win your business, but expect to pay more per unit.

faqs.q: Do I need to speak Chinese to work with a Chinese supplier?
faqs.a: No, you can manage in English. But if you want to avoid misunderstandings, especially on calls or in WeChat chats, you can hire an interpreter. pages.title: What Does MOQ Mean and How to Negotiate It
pages.desc: MOQ means minimum order quantity. Learn why suppliers quote high MOQs first and the specific asks that move them down.
pages.target_query: what does moq mean and how to negotiate it
pages.text: MOQ stands for minimum order quantity, the smallest amount a supplier will produce or sell in one order. Suppliers quote high MOQs first because it protects their production efficiency and profit margin. To move it, you need to ask the right specific questions. A supplier's first MOQ is rarely their final number. They start high because a larger run means lower per-unit cost, fewer changeovers, and more predictable revenue for their factory. It also filters out buyers who are not serious or who cannot commit. The quoted MOQ is often a starting point for negotiation, not a fixed rule. Factories have flexibility, especially when they have spare capacity or want to fill a production slot. Understanding their cost structure helps you make a counteroffer that works for both sides. Instead of asking 'Can you lower the MOQ?', ask targeted questions. For example, ask if the MOQ applies to the whole order or per color and size. Ask if you can start with a trial order at a higher unit price to test the market. Another effective ask is to negotiate a phased delivery: order the full MOQ but receive it in batches. This reduces your upfront risk while keeping the supplier's production run intact. You can also ask about leftover stock or off-season production, which often comes with lower MOQs. In Chinese, MOQ is often expressed as 起订量 (qǐ dìng liàng), which means 'starting order quantity'. When a supplier quotes a high 起订量, they are telling you the minimum they are willing to produce for that price. Lowering the MOQ usually means raising the unit price. Knowing the term helps you communicate directly with suppliers. If you work with an interpreter, you can ask precise questions about 起订量 and how it changes with price. This clarity prevents misunderstandings and shows the supplier you understand their logic. Start by asking for the MOQ breakdown: per product, per color, per size. Then ask if the MOQ can be reduced if you accept a higher price. Many suppliers will accept a 20-30% lower MOQ for a 5-10% price increase, but you have to ask. Also ask about payment terms. Offering a larger deposit or faster payment can give you leverage to lower the MOQ. Suppliers value cash flow, so a 50% deposit upfront might make them more flexible on quantity. Some suppliers will not budge on MOQ, especially for custom-made products or tight profit margins. If the MOQ is truly fixed, you have options: find a supplier with a lower MOQ, join a group buy with other small importers, or use a sourcing platform that aggregates demand. Another option is to buy from a trading company that buys from multiple factories and can split orders. They often have lower MOQs than the factory itself. pages.text: Chinese New Year shipping delays happen because factories close for two to four weeks, not just a few days. The entire supply chain—from production to freight—slows down or stops. If you plan backwards from your target delivery date and ask the right questions in November, you can avoid the worst of it. Chinese New Year (春节, chūnjié, Spring Festival) is the most important holiday in China. Workers travel home to be with family, and factories shut down completely. This is not a short break: most production lines stop for at least two weeks, and many for a month or more. The shutdown affects more than just the factory floor. Suppliers stop taking new orders, raw material deliveries halt, and logistics providers reduce staff. Even after the factory reopens, it takes days to restart production and catch up on backlogged orders. Many buyers assume a few days of closure, but the reality is longer. The official holiday is usually 7 days, but most factories extend it to 2-3 weeks because workers need travel time and many take extra leave. Add the pre-holiday rush and post-holiday ramp-up, and you are looking at 4-6 weeks of reduced output. For example, if Chinese New Year falls in late January, you should assume no production from mid-January to mid-February. If you order in December, your goods may not ship until March. That is why planning backwards from your target date is critical. November is the time to ask specific questions, not just 'when is your holiday?' Add the pre-holiday rush and post-holiday ramp-up, and you are looking at 4-6 weeks of reduced output.

For example, if Chinese New Year falls in late January, you should assume no production from mid-January to mid-February. If you order in December, your goods may not ship until March. That is why planning backwards from your target date is critical.
bullets: Official holiday: 7 days (usually).
Actual factory closure: 2-4 weeks.
Full recovery to normal output: up to 6 weeks.

sections.h2: What to Ask Your Supplier in November
body: November is the time to ask specific questions, not just 'when is your holiday?' You need to know exact closure dates, last order dates, and production lead times. Ask in writing and get answers in writing.

If you are working with a Chinese supplier and need help understanding the answers, a live interpreter can clarify what they really mean. Renata, for example, offers remote message support and live calls to help you read between the lines.
Here are the questions to ask:
What are your exact closure dates? (春节放假日期, chūnjié fàngjià rìqī, Chinese New Year holiday dates)
What is the last day to place an order before the holiday? (最晚下单日期, zuìwǎn xiàdān rìqī, latest order date)
What is the production lead time for my product? (生产周期, shēngchǎn zhōuqī, production cycle)
Will you have staff available during the holiday for urgent questions? (假期有值班人员吗, jiàqī yǒu zhíbān rényuán ma, are there duty staff during the holiday?)
What is your shipping cutoff before the holiday? (节前发货截止日期, jié qián fāhuò jiézhǐ rìqī, pre-holiday shipping deadline)
bullets: Ask for exact dates, not just 'we close for a week'.
Get written confirmation of lead times.
Clarify what happens if your order is late.

sections.h2: Plan Backwards from Your Target Date
body: Start with the date you need the goods in your warehouse or at your customer's door. Work backwards: add shipping time (ocean or air), customs clearance, and production time. Then add a buffer of at least 2 weeks for Chinese New Year disruption.

For example, if you need goods by March 1, and ocean shipping takes 30 days, production takes 20 days, and customs takes 5 days, you need to start production by late January. That means you must place your order in early January at the latest—but many factories stop taking orders in December. So you actually need to order in November.
This is why November is the critical month. If you wait until December, you may be too late.

sections.h2: What If You Miss the Window?
body: If you miss the pre-holiday ordering window, you have a few options. You can wait until after the holiday, but that means delays of 4-6 weeks. You can pay for air freight instead of ocean, but that is much more expensive. Or you can find a supplier that stays open, but that is rare and often unreliable.
The best strategy is to avoid the problem entirely by planning ahead. If you are already in a bind, be honest with your supplier and ask for realistic timelines. Do not expect miracles.
Renata can help you communicate these urgent requests, but she cannot guarantee a supplier's response or speed. She is not a sourcing agent and does not control factory schedules.

faqs.q: How long do Chinese factories close for Chinese New Year?
faqs.a: Most factories close for 2 to 4 weeks, not just the official 7-day holiday. Workers need travel time and often take extra leave, so production stops well before and after the holiday. Plan for at least a month of reduced output.

faqs.q: When should I place my order to avoid Chinese New Year delays?
faqs.a: Place your order in November, at the latest early December. Factories stop taking new orders 2-4 weeks before the holiday, and production slots fill up fast. Ordering in November gives you time to confirm details and secure a production slot before the shutdown.

faqs.q: What questions should I ask my supplier about Chinese New Year?
faqs.a: Ask for exact closure dates, the last day to place an order, production lead time, shipping cutoff, and whether any staff will be available during the holiday. Get all answers in writing to avoid misunderstandings.

faqs.q: Can I still order in December and get goods before Chinese New Year?
faqs.a: It is risky. Many factories stop accepting orders in December because they are already at full capacity. Even if you order, production may not start until after the holiday. You might get lucky with air freight, but do not count on it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the official holiday and actual factory closure?
faqs.a: The official holiday is usually 7 days, but factories often close longer. Workers travel home and return slowly, so production may not resume fully for 2-4 weeks. Always ask for the actual closure dates, not the official ones.

faqs.q: Does Renata help with ordering or finding suppliers?
faqs.a: No, Renata is not a sourcing agent and does not find suppliers or inspect factories. She provides live interpreting and message support to help you communicate with Chinese suppliers. She can clarify what a supplier means, but she does not handle logistics or quality control.
